name: Change Blindness
description: People are strikingly poor at detecting even large changes to a scene when the moment of change itself is masked (e.g. by a blink, cut, or blank flash), because attention, not raw visual exposure, is what makes a change perceptible from one glance to the next.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to interface transitions and live-updating dashboards: a state change that isn't paired with an attention cue (motion, highlight, animation) risks going unnoticed even when it's visually large.
prevalence_note: Recognized in interaction-design and dashboard/data-viz discourse specifically (justifying animated transitions on state change), though not as universally cited outside that niche as e.g. anchoring or scarcity.

findings.description: When a brief blank field masks the motion transient between an original and a modified scene, observers become strikingly poor at detecting even large, repeated changes; detection is much faster when a verbal cue names the changed object or when the changed object is of high semantic interest in the scene — evidence that attention, not raw visibility, gates change perception, and that people do not hold a complete detailed representation of a scene from one glance to the next.
findings.source_title: To See or Not to See: The Need for Attention to Perceive Changes in Scenes

applications.title: Southwest's near-invisible loading spinner vs. Kayak's contrasting one -- the same UI element, noticed or not
applications.description: In a Nielsen Norman Group article (Kathryn Whitenton, March 29, 2015), the Southwest Airlines app's animated progress indicator is placed in the exact center of the screen but is, in the article's own words, 'almost impossible to distinguish' -- a real interface change that most users' attention simply passes over, a direct instance of change blindness. By contrast, a similar progress indicator on Kayak.com is noticeable specifically because it sits on a contrasting background element that separates it visually from the rest of the page. The same article separately notes a 'Data Transfer Error' notification on a GoodSourcing.com registration form that can likewise be easily overlooked because its visual treatment blends into the surrounding page rather than standing out.
applications.industry_context: Travel booking (Southwest's native app and Kayak's website), contrasted directly by the source as the same interface pattern implemented well and poorly.
applications.ethical_note: A pure attention/perception design issue with no persuasive or manipulative dimension -- the failure mode actively works against both the user's and the business's interest (a user who doesn't notice a loading state or an error can't act on it), so there's no benefit-to-someone-at-another's-expense question to grade here.
